entries.narration: Every model in this course is a parameterised function: it takes an input, here a photograph of a part from the workshop's inspection station, and maps it to an output, here scores for three classes, ok, scratch and dent. What distinguishes a neural network is where its features come from. In the classical route, a person designs the features: count the edges, measure the brightness, describe the texture, and then a model such as logistic regression learns how much weight to give each one. In the neural route, the features themselves are parameters. A hidden layer takes the raw pixels and computes its own description of the image, and training adjusts that layer at the same time as the output layer. That hidden description is called a representation, and learning good representations is the central idea of deep learning. The code shows the tiny classifier we will use: flatten the image to twelve thousand two hundred and eighty-eight numbers, map them to thirty-two hidden features, then to three class scores. That is three hundred and ninety-three thousand three hundred and forty-seven parameters, nearly all in the first layer. More parameters are more to learn, not a promise of a better model.

Every model family builds in an assumption about the data, called its inductive bias, and on this task the assumption matters far more than the parameter count. The table compares four candidates on the same validation split, made by production batch, scored by macro-averaged F1 across the three classes. Always predicting the most common class gives nought point two seven: the floor. Twelve hand-designed features with logistic regression reach nought point seven one, with only thirty-nine parameters. The fully connected network on raw pixels, with nearly four hundred thousand parameters, does slightly worse, nought point six nine. Its bias is a poor fit: it treats every pixel as an unrelated input, so a scratch shifted by one pixel looks like a completely new pattern, and it has to learn the same scratch at every position separately. A small convolutional network, about twenty-four thousand parameters, reaches nought point eight six, because it assumes that useful patterns are local and repeat across the image, which is exactly what defects do. Chapter six explains how. The lesson for now is that a neural approach is a hypothesis to be tested against a baseline, on the same split, not a default.

Neural computation is written in tensors, which here simply means multidimensional arrays of numbers. Three facts describe a tensor well enough to reason about it. The first is its shape, the size of each axis. A batch of thirty-two colour images, sixty-four pixels square, is a tensor of shape thirty-two, three, sixty-four, sixty-four, and the axes mean, in order, which image, which colour channel, which row and which column. That ordering, often written N C H W, is a convention, and other libraries put the channels last, so an axis's meaning is something to write down, not assume. The batch holds three hundred and ninety-three thousand two hundred and sixteen numbers, while its labels are a single axis of thirty-two class indices. The second fact is the dtype. Thirty-two-bit floats take four bytes each, so this batch is about one and a half mebibytes, and sixteen-bit floats would halve that. Labels for classification are sixty-four-bit integers, indices rather than numbers to average. The third fact is the device: whether the tensor lives in CPU memory or on a GPU. Every tensor in one operation must be on the same device, and moving between them takes time.

Most shape mistakes stop the program with an error, which is the good case. The dangerous ones run, and quietly return the wrong number. The first is accidental broadcasting. Broadcasting is the rule that lets a tensor with a size-one axis be stretched to match another, which is genuinely useful, for example to add a bias to every row. But suppose a model outputs predictions with shape three by one, and the targets have shape three. Subtracting them does not pair each prediction with its own target; it broadcasts to a three-by-three matrix comparing every prediction with every target. The table computes it. The predictions here are perfect, so the true mean squared error is zero, but the broadcast version averages all nine pairs and reports one point three three. Nothing crashes. The fix is to make the shapes identical before computing the loss, and to assert that they are. The second mistake is using reshape when you mean permute. Moving channels to the last axis with permute keeps each pixel's channel values together. Reshape only reinterprets the same memory in a new shape, so pixel nought, one ends up with values three and four, which belong to different pixels.

Neural networks process data in batches, and a batch is a single tensor, so it has to be a rectangle. Ragged inputs therefore need a rule. For text fragments, the rule is padding. Here three fragments of three, five and one tokens are padded with a special PAD token to a batch of shape three by five, and alongside them goes a mask, one for real tokens and zero for padding. The padding is a convenience for storage; it carries no information, so every later step that sums or averages over tokens has to use the mask, or the padding silently contaminates the result. Chapter two shows exactly that failure in a loss. For images, the rule is usually to resize every image to one shape, here sixty-four by sixty-four, and that is a modelling choice too, because resizing can blur a fine scratch. Together these rules make up a data contract that every batch must meet: the shape, the dtype and the value range, one fixed mapping from label names to indices, and normalisation statistics such as the mean pixel value, computed on training data only. The contract is not just for training. The same rules have to hold at prediction time.

A neural model needs exactly the same prediction contract as any model from the Machine Learning course, and image data makes some of the leaks especially easy to miss. The unit is one part, photographed at the inspection station before it is packed, and the only input is that image, because the prediction has to be made at that moment. The target is ok, scratch or dent, as labelled by an inspector, and the decision it supports is whether to route the part for a manual check. The labels are not perfect: when two inspectors labelled the same images, they disagreed on eight percent, and that uncertainty belongs in the contract, because no model can be more reliable than the labels it is scored against. Then the boundaries. Images from one production batch share lighting, camera position and material lot, so if images from the same batch land on both sides of a split, the model can recognise the batch rather than the defect. The split is therefore by batch. The station also takes burst photos, near-duplicates of the same part, which a random split would scatter across training and test. And rework notes or customer returns arrive later, so they can never be inputs.

This section sets up the notation used for the rest of the course. In PyTorch, a model is a module: its layers are created in the constructor, and the computation is written in the forward method. Our defect classifier has two linear layers. The first maps the twelve thousand two hundred and eighty-eight pixel values to thirty-two hidden features; the second maps those thirty-two features to three class scores. Flatten one keeps the batch axis and flattens everything after it into one long vector per image. The forward method returns logits, raw unnormalised scores, and deliberately does not apply a softmax; chapter two explains why the loss should do that. The habit worth adopting from day one is shape discipline. Put a comment on every line saying what shape it produces, and put assertions at the boundaries, so that a mismatch fails loudly at the point where it happens rather than surfacing later as a strange number. The table is the trace those comments promise: thirty-two images of three by sixty-four by sixty-four become thirty-two vectors of twelve thousand, then thirty-two hidden vectors of thirty-two, then thirty-two rows of three logits, lined up with thirty-two integer labels.

A neural network layer does two things. First an affine map: multiply the input by a weight matrix and add a bias vector. Then an activation function, applied separately to every element of the result. The activation is not decoration; without it, depth means nothing. The table shows why, with small concrete matrices. Stack two affine layers with nothing between them, and the composition is W two times W one x plus b one, plus b two, which rearranges into a single matrix W two W one times x, plus a single bias. Computed here, the two-layer stack is exactly the one-layer function y equals one, one dot x plus one point five. However many affine layers you stack, you get one affine layer. Put a nonlinear function between them and that collapse no longer happens, which is what lets composition build richer functions. The plot shows the usual choices. ReLU, the maximum of zero and its input, is cheap and the default in most vision models, but its gradient is zero for negative inputs. GELU is a smooth version used in transformers. Sigmoid and tanh flatten out at both ends, and that saturation can stall learning, which chapter four returns to.

Here is a complete forward pass you can check by hand. XOR outputs one when exactly one of its two inputs is one. Plot the four inputs and you see the problem: the two ones sit on one diagonal and the two zeros on the other, so no single straight line separates them, and no linear model can compute XOR. Now add one hidden layer of two ReLU units. The first computes relu of x one plus x two. The second computes relu of x one plus x two minus one. The output is the first hidden unit minus twice the second. Trace each input through the table. Zero, zero gives zero everywhere. Zero, one and one, zero both give a first hidden value of one and a second of zero, so the output is one. One, one gives two and one, and two minus two is zero. Exactly XOR. What the hidden layer did was move the four points into a new space where a line does separate them, which is the idea of a learned representation in its smallest form. Counting parameters: each layer has inputs times outputs weights, plus one bias per output, nine in total. These weights were chosen by hand; training has to find such weights from data.

Capacity can be added by making layers wider or by stacking more of them, and the costs are very different. For a fully connected network on sixty-four by sixty-four colour images, the first layer dominates everything, because it connects every one of twelve thousand two hundred and eighty-eight inputs to every hidden unit. A single hidden layer of two hundred and fifty-six units costs over three million parameters. Narrowing it to thirty-two cuts that to under four hundred thousand. And stacking seven more thirty-two-wide layers on top costs only about seven thousand four hundred more, because each extra layer is only thirty-two by thirty-two. There is a famous result behind all this, the universal approximation theorem: a single hidden layer, made wide enough, can approximate any continuous function as closely as you like. It is true, and it is much less useful than it sounds. It says nothing about how wide is wide enough, which can be enormous, nothing about how much data you would need, and nothing about whether training would find those weights. In practice depth often helps because later layers can reuse and combine features computed earlier. Deep stacks have training problems of their own, which chapters four and six address.

The output layer of a network is called its head, and choosing it is not a matter of taste: the target decides the head, and the head decides the loss. The same workshop can ask four different questions. How long is the scratch, in millimetres? That is regression: one raw output and a squared-error loss. Is there any defect at all? That is binary: one logit, and the binary cross-entropy loss that takes logits directly. Is the part ok, scratched or dented? That is multiclass, exactly one class per image: three logits and cross-entropy, with the targets given as integer class indices. Could a part be both scratched and dented? That is multilabel: three logits, each with its own sigmoid, each answered independently, again with binary cross-entropy but now against a row of zeros and ones. The dangerous part is that mismatches often run without error. Pass one-hot float targets where indices are expected, apply a softmax or sigmoid yourself before a loss that already does it, or give a target of shape N against an output of shape N by one, and training proceeds, the loss goes down, and the model learns something other than you intended.

A multiclass head outputs logits, one raw score per class, which can be any real numbers. Softmax turns them into probabilities: exponentiate each, then divide by the total, so they are positive and add up to one. Take one image with logits two, nought point five and minus one, for ok, scratch and dent. Softmax gives nought point seven eight six, nought point one seven five and nought point zero three nine. Cross-entropy looks only at the probability assigned to the true class and takes minus its logarithm. If this image really is ok, the loss is nought point two four one, small, because the model was fairly confident and right. If it is actually scratched, the loss is one point seven four. If it is dented, three point two four, because the model gave that class under four percent. Averaged over a batch, this is the negative log-likelihood of the labels under the model, the probability theory belonging to the statistics course, and minimising it pushes the predicted probabilities toward the frequencies seen in the data. In PyTorch, the cross-entropy function takes logits and applies its own log-softmax internally. Passing in probabilities you have already softmaxed applies softmax twice, which runs, and quietly trains worse.

The softmax formula as usually written exponentiates the logits directly, and that breaks on large values. The exponential of one thousand is far beyond what any floating-point format can hold, so it becomes infinity, and infinity divided by infinity is not a number. One NaN in a loss spreads to every gradient and every weight within a step. The fix costs nothing. Softmax is unchanged if you subtract the same constant from every logit, so subtract the largest one first. Logits of one thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine and nine hundred and ninety-eight become zero, minus one and minus two, which exponentiate safely and give probabilities of nought point six six five, nought point two four five and nought point zero nine. The log of the denominator, called log-sum-exp, is computed the same way: the maximum plus the log of the shifted sum. Then there is the reduction, how per-example losses become one number. Mean keeps the gradient's scale independent of batch size. Sum makes it grow with the batch, so a learning rate tuned at one batch size no longer fits another. None keeps every example's loss, for masking or weighting. The built-in losses already use the stable forms, which is a good reason to prefer them.

Every reduced loss is an average over something, and it pays to check what. Here are per-token losses for two text fragments padded to the same length. The second fragment has only one real token; its other two positions are padding. Padding is trivially easy to predict, so the model's loss there is tiny, nought point zero one. Average over all six positions and the loss reads nought point three seven. Average over the four real tokens and it is nought point five five. The unmasked number is not just wrong; it improves whenever batches contain more padding, so it rewards nothing real, and its gradients push effort toward predicting pads. The fix is to compute per-token losses with no reduction, multiply by the mask, and divide by the number of real tokens, or to tell the loss which index to ignore. Weighted and multi-head objectives raise the same question. A network can have a defect-class head and a scratch-length head sharing one body, trained on cross-entropy plus a half times the length error. That half is a modelling choice that trades one task against the other. And the loss is for training: report each head with its own metric, separately.

Backpropagation is the chain rule, applied systematically to a graph of simple operations. Here is the network we will trace all chapter: two inputs, a hidden layer of two ReLU units, one output, and a squared-error loss against a target of one. Written as a graph, it is a chain of four operations. The affine map makes z one from x. ReLU makes h from z one. A second affine map makes the output y. And the loss compares y with the target. The crucial property is that each operation only needs to know its own local derivative. The loss knows that its derivative with respect to y is y minus t. The output layer knows its derivative with respect to h is just its weight vector. ReLU knows its derivative is one where its input was positive and zero elsewhere. Run the forward pass with the weights shown and the output is minus nought point one eight, a loss of nought point six nine six. Notice that the local derivatives need forward values: ReLU's needs z one, and the weight gradient needs x. That is why the forward pass stores them, and why training uses more memory than inference. The chain rule then multiplies local derivatives along the path back to each parameter.

Now run the chain backward. It starts at the loss: the derivative with respect to y is y minus t, minus one point one eight. The output layer's weights each multiplied one hidden value, so their gradients are that upstream gradient times the hidden values: minus nought point one one eight and minus one point zero six two. The output bias was simply added, so its gradient is the upstream gradient itself. To continue into the network we need the gradient with respect to h, which is the upstream gradient times the output weights: minus nought point eight two six and nought point five nine. Next comes ReLU. Both hidden pre-activations were positive, so ReLU's local derivative is one for both, and the gradient passes through unchanged. Had either been negative, its gradient would have been blocked to zero, and that unit's incoming weights would get no update from this example. Finally the first-layer weights: each gradient is the hidden unit's gradient times the input it multiplied, an outer product of the two vectors. Three patterns repeat in every network: a weight's gradient is upstream times input, a bias's gradient is the upstream gradient, and every gradient has the same shape as its parameter.

The last section traced the chain rule by hand, layer by layer. Automatic differentiation does exactly the same thing, and it is worth seeing why it runs backward. Training needs the gradient of one number, the loss, with respect to every parameter, often millions of them. At each step of the backward pass, we hold the gradient of the loss with respect to some intermediate result, a row vector, and we multiply it by that operation's local Jacobian, the matrix of its partial derivatives. That product is called a vector-Jacobian product, and it can almost always be computed without ever building the Jacobian itself, which would be enormous. Because we start from a single scalar, one backward sweep produces the gradient for every parameter at once. Compare the alternatives. Forward-mode differentiation pushes derivatives from the inputs toward the output and needs one pass per parameter. Finite differences need two forward passes per parameter and are only approximate. Reverse mode costs roughly one extra forward pass in time, and pays for it in memory by keeping the forward activations. PyTorch exposes the primitive directly: autograd grad with grad outputs computes a vector-Jacobian product.

Often a single parameter is used in more than one place, and then its gradient is the sum of the contributions from every use. Take the smallest possible case: one weight w multiplies two different inputs, and the results are added. With w equal to a half and inputs two and three, the output is two and a half, and against a target of one the loss gradient with respect to the output is one and a half. Follow each path back to w. Through the first use, the contribution is one and a half times two, which is three. Through the second, one and a half times three, which is four and a half. The gradient of the loss with respect to w is their sum, seven and a half. This is just the multivariable chain rule: when a variable affects the output along several paths, you add the derivatives along each path. It matters because sharing is everywhere in deep learning. A convolution filter is applied at every position in an image, a recurrent cell at every step of a sequence, and a body with two output heads receives a gradient from each head. Autograd sums all of these automatically. A hand-written backward pass has to as well, or it silently loses information.

A batch's gradient is assembled from the gradients of its individual examples, and the loss reduction decides how. Take one weight and a batch of four examples whose separate gradients are nought point eight, minus nought point two, nought point five and nought point one. With the default mean reduction, the loss is the average over the batch, so the weight's gradient is the average of the four: nought point three. With sum reduction, it is their total, one point two, four times larger, and it would be eight times larger with a batch of eight. That matters because the learning rate multiplies the gradient. A learning rate tuned with mean reduction is far too large under sum, and a sum-based setup does not transfer between batch sizes. The same trap appears with gradient accumulation, where a large batch is processed as several smaller micro-batches. Split our four examples into two micro-batches of two, compute a mean loss on each, and call backward on both without clearing: the accumulated gradient is nought point six, twice the true mean. The fix is to divide each micro-batch's loss by the number of accumulation steps. Whenever batch size or accumulation changes, check the gradient's scale.

Autograd works by recording. Whenever an operation involves a tensor that requires gradients, it adds a node to the graph and saves whatever that operation will need during backward; sigmoid, for instance, saves its own output. Parameters are leaves: tensors created with requires grad set, whose gradients accumulate in their grad attribute. You control the record in a few ways. Detach returns a tensor with the same values and no gradient path, which is exactly what you want for a target produced by a frozen teacher model: you use its numbers, but no gradient should flow into it. The no-grad context records nothing at all inside its block, which saves memory when you only need predictions. The hazards come from changing tensors behind autograd's back. In the code, sigmoid saved its output h, and then h is doubled in place. When backward runs, the value it saved has changed, and PyTorch raises an error rather than compute a wrong gradient. Code that bypasses this check, for example by editing the data attribute, gets wrong gradients silently. Converting to NumPy also leaves the graph. And a parameter whose grad is still None after backward was cut off from the loss somewhere.

Here is one of the most common bugs in hand-written training loops. Calling backward does not replace the contents of a parameter's grad; it adds to them. That design is deliberate, because it is what makes shared weights and gradient accumulation work, but it means a training loop has to clear the gradients itself before each new backward pass. Suppose a weight's true gradients over four steps are nought point six, nought point five, nought point four five and nought point four. With the gradients cleared each step, grad holds exactly those values. Forget to clear them, and grad holds the running sum instead: nought point six, then one point one, then one point five five, then one point nine five. Every update now uses a larger and more out-of-date gradient than it should, so training drifts or blows up, and nothing anywhere raises an error; the loss curve just looks strange. Sometimes accumulation is exactly what you want: to imitate a batch too large to fit in memory, call backward on several micro-batches before taking one optimiser step. Scale each micro-batch's loss by the number of steps, step once, and then clear. Setting gradients to None, rather than to zero, saves memory and makes accidental reuse fail loudly.

When you write your own gradient, for a custom layer or an unusual loss, you can check it against the definition of a derivative. Nudge one parameter up by a small epsilon, recompute the loss, nudge it down by epsilon, recompute again, and divide the difference by two epsilon. That central difference approximates the derivative with respect to that parameter. For the chapter network, with epsilon one in ten thousand, the backward pass and the finite differences agree to about one part in ten to the thirteen for every parameter checked, which is as close as double precision allows. Compare using relative error rather than absolute, and expect much weaker agreement in single precision, which is why PyTorch's gradient checker runs in double precision. The check has one important blind spot: points where the function has no derivative. ReLU has a kink at zero. A central difference centred exactly there averages a slope of zero on the left and one on the right, and reports a half. PyTorch's convention is to use zero at that point. Neither number is wrong, because there is no derivative to get right; it just means a numerical check should be run at points away from kinks.

Chapter three computed gradients; a training loop uses them, and in doing so it changes several different kinds of state. The loop itself is short. Put the model in training mode. For each batch, run the forward pass, compute the loss, clear the old gradients, run backward to fill in new ones, let the optimiser update the parameters, and advance the learning-rate schedule. What is easy to miss is how much state that loop is carrying. The parameters are the obvious part, the weights and biases the optimiser changes. Then there are buffers, such as batch normalisation's running mean and variance, which chapter six explains; they are updated by the forward pass in training mode, not by gradients, but they are part of the model and are saved with it. The optimiser has its own state: momentum keeps a running velocity for every weight, and Adam keeps two running moments for every weight, so for Adam the optimiser state is twice the size of the model. The schedule knows the current learning rate and step. And randomness, the shuffle order and the dropout masks, comes from random number generators with states of their own. Each piece is saved separately, which is exactly how they get lost.

Two switches are often confused because they are usually flipped together. Calling eval on a model changes how certain layers behave. Dropout, which in training zeroes a random thirty percent of its inputs and scales the rest up to compensate, becomes the identity. Batch normalisation stops using the current batch's statistics and stops updating its running averages, and uses those stored averages instead. Linear layers, convolutions and ReLU are unaffected. The no-grad context does something else entirely: it tells autograd not to record operations, so no graph is built, memory use falls, and backward is impossible. Neither implies the other, so all four combinations exist. Training mode with recording is an ordinary training step. Eval mode under no grad is validation and inference. Eval mode with recording is legitimate too, for example computing gradients with respect to the input image while keeping batch norm frozen. The fourth combination, training mode under no grad, is the classic bug: validation numbers come out noisy because dropout is still active, and worse, every validation batch quietly updates the batch-norm statistics with data the model is supposed to be judged on. And remember to switch back to training mode afterwards.

A training run produces a sequence of models, one per epoch, and we have to choose which one to keep. Training loss is no guide: it falls every epoch, heading toward about nought point one five, because the model keeps fitting its training images more closely. Validation loss tells the real story. It falls at first, reaches its lowest point at epoch seventeen, nought point four one one, and then rises as the model starts to memorise the training images instead of learning defects in general. So we keep the epoch-seventeen weights, not the last ones. This is the same selection logic as the Machine Learning course, applied to training time. The chosen epoch is a choice made by looking at validation data, so its validation score is selection evidence and is somewhat optimistic. The validation split must respect the same boundaries as the final test, here split by production batch, or the choice is tuned to batches it has already seen. And the test set is opened exactly once, after the checkpoint, the architecture and every training setting are fixed. When saving the chosen checkpoint, save the full state, model, optimiser, schedule, epoch and random states, which the last section of this chapter shows the reason for.

The optimiser decides how a gradient becomes a step. Take one weight equal to one, a gradient of a half, a learning rate of nought point one and a decay strength of one hundredth, and compute a single step under each rule. Plain stochastic gradient descent subtracts the learning rate times the gradient: nought point nine five. Momentum, not shown, would also blend in recent gradients, smoothing out noisy directions. Adam keeps running estimates of each weight's gradient and squared gradient, and divides one by the square root of the other, so its step size is roughly the learning rate regardless of the gradient's scale. On the first step that gives exactly nought point nine. Now weight decay, where the subtlety lies. For plain SGD, adding an L2 penalty to the loss and shrinking the weights directly are the same thing: nought point nine four nine. For Adam they are not. Adding L2 means adding lambda times w to the gradient, and Adam then normalises the whole gradient, so on this first step the decay disappears entirely: still nought point nine. AdamW decouples the decay, shrinking the weight directly, and gives nought point eight nine nine. So Adam with L2 and AdamW are not interchangeable, and a decay setting tuned for one does not transfer to the other.

Initialisation decides whether a deep network can be trained at all. Think about the spread of activations as a signal passes forward through many layers. For ReLU layers of width n, with weights drawn at standard deviation sigma, each layer multiplies the variance of the activations by n times sigma squared over two, so after ten layers that factor has been applied ten times. The plot computes it for a width of two hundred and fifty-six. With sigma one hundredth, the factor is far below one and the activations shrink toward zero within a few layers. With sigma one tenth, it is above one and they blow up. Kaiming initialisation chooses sigma as the square root of two over n, which makes the factor exactly one, and the spread stays steady through every layer. Gradients travelling backward obey the same kind of scaling, so a bad start means vanishing or exploding gradients too. Initialisation also has to break symmetry. If two hidden units start with identical weights, they compute identical outputs, receive identical gradients, here minus nought point zero five and minus nought point one each, and receive identical updates, forever. They never become different features. Random initialisation breaks the tie.

Two tools shape the steps beyond the optimiser's own rule. The first is the learning-rate schedule. A common pattern starts with warmup, raising the learning rate linearly from zero over the first five hundred steps, which gives Adam's running moment estimates time to settle before large steps are taken. Then cosine decay lowers the rate smoothly toward zero by the end of training, so the final steps are small and refine rather than disrupt. The schedule is part of the experiment's setup, and because it is defined over the total number of steps, changing the training length changes the schedule too. The second tool is gradient clipping. Clipping by global norm measures the size of the entire gradient across all parameters and, if it exceeds a limit, rescales it. A gradient of norm twelve, clipped to one, is multiplied by one twelfth; every component shrinks by the same factor, so the direction is unchanged and only the step length is capped. Clipping protects against a single bad batch, but it can also hide a real problem, so log how often it fires. In general, log the loss and stop on NaN, the gradient norm, the learning rate actually in use, and the share of ReLU units that never activate.

Setting a random seed makes the random choices in a run repeatable: the initial weights, the shuffle order, the dropout masks. To do that properly, seed Python, NumPy and PyTorch, and give the data loader its own seeded generator and worker seeds, because loaders shuffle and augment in separate processes. Seeds alone are not enough, though, because some GPU operations are nondeterministic by design: they add floating-point numbers in whatever order threads finish, and floating-point addition is not associative. The table shows three runs with the same seed, same code and same data on one GPU. With default kernels, the validation scores differ in the third decimal place. Requesting deterministic algorithms makes all three identical, at some cost in speed, and PyTorch raises an error if an operation has no deterministic version. Even then, a different GPU model or a new library version can change results, so record the environment. The most important line is the last one. Across five different seeds the mean is nought point eight five seven with a standard deviation of nought point zero zero six. That spread is the real uncertainty in a single run's score, and it is the reason to report several seeds rather than one.

Long runs get interrupted, and resuming one correctly needs all of its state. The plot shows a run stopped at step two thousand and resumed two ways. Restored with the model, optimiser and schedule state, the training loss carries on as if nothing had happened. Restored with only the model weights, the loss jumps. Adam's running moment estimates have been reset to zero, so its first steps after the restart are scaled as if training had just begun, and the schedule may restart its warmup or sit at the wrong learning rate. The model recovers eventually, but it is no longer the same run, and any comparison with an uninterrupted run is muddied. The fix is to save and restore everything together: model, optimiser, schedule, the step count and the random states. The second half of this section is about naming failures correctly, because their remedies differ. If training loss will not fall, it is an optimisation failure, and the suspects are the learning rate, initialisation, the gradients themselves, or a broken data pipeline. If training loss falls but validation loss does not, it is a generalisation failure, the subject of the next chapter. Changing the regulariser will not fix an optimiser problem, and the reverse.

Neural networks generalise in ways that classical capacity arguments do not fully explain, and this chapter is about the evidence we can actually gather. Start with learning curves, validation macro F1 against the number of training images, on the same batch-split folds. The small CNN keeps improving as data grows; the MLP flattens out early, because its lack of spatial bias wastes the extra images. Both stay below a ceiling that has nothing to do with the model: two inspectors labelling the same images agree only ninety-two percent of the time, and no model can be scored above the consistency of its labels. Where a curve is still rising at the right-hand end, more data is the remedy worth pricing. Now a striking experiment. Train the same CNN on the same images, but shuffle the labels at random, so there is nothing real to learn. It still reaches perfect training accuracy: it simply memorises which image goes with which label. Validation accuracy falls to a third, chance for three classes. So a network's capacity is large enough to fit anything, which means a perfect training score proves nothing, and noisy labels get partly memorised too. Generalisation evidence has to come from held-out data.

Three regularisers are standard in neural networks, and each restrains the model differently. Dropout is the most distinctive. In training mode, every activation is independently set to zero with some probability, here a quarter, and the survivors are scaled up by one over three quarters. Traced on the vector one, two, three, four with the second element dropped, the output is one point three three, zero, four, and five point three three. The scaling keeps the expected value of every element unchanged, so the next layer sees inputs of the same average size in training and in evaluation. In evaluation mode dropout does nothing at all. Because a unit cannot rely on any particular other unit being present, the network is pushed toward redundant, more robust features. Weight decay shrinks weights toward zero, and as chapter four showed, with Adam it should be decoupled. Early stopping simply halts at the best validation epoch. On the defect CNN, with no regulariser, training macro F1 is nought point nine nine and validation nought point eight, a gap of nought point one nine. Each regulariser narrows the gap, and all three together bring it to six hundredths. These are averages over three seeds, so differences under a hundredth are noise.

Augmentation enlarges the training set by transforming existing images: flip them, rotate them slightly, change the brightness. It works when the transformation keeps the label true. A horizontal flip of a scratched part is still a scratched part. A rotation of ten degrees matches how camera mountings vary. A brightness change matches the lighting. But some common transforms change the label without saying so. A random crop that keeps half the image can cut the scratch out entirely, leaving an image labelled scratch that shows no scratch, and the model is taught that clean metal sometimes means scratched. A heavy blur erases fine scratches in the same way. Augmentation is applied to training images only, never to validation or test. The second half of this section is about shortcuts, which augmentation alone does not fix. Our model scores nought point nine one on validation images from the same stations, which looks excellent. On a newly installed station it scores nought point six two. The reason: in the training data, dented parts had mostly been photographed on the grey rework bench, and the model learned to recognise the bench. With the background masked, it scores nought point eight five. Test on data that breaks the shortcut.

Neural networks have far more choices than classical models: learning rate, width, depth, dropout, schedule, batch size, and more. With that many, a search can always find a setting that looks good on validation by luck, so the search is declared before it runs. Here each model family gets the same budget of twenty trials of random search, over the learning rate on a log scale, the width and the dropout rate, all scored on the same three folds grouped by production batch. The best configuration from each family is then retrained with five different seeds. The table shows why that last step matters. The best single trial for the small CNN scored nought point eight seven, but that trial was selected for being the best, so it is optimistic. Re-run with five seeds, the same configuration scores nought point eight six, give or take a hundredth. Adding batch normalisation won its best trial at nought point eight eight, but across seeds it ties with the plain CNN, while costing half as much compute again. When two candidates tie within seed noise, prefer the cheaper one. And report each family's budget and compute alongside its score, so that a heavily tuned favourite is not mistaken for a better architecture.

When a network performs badly, it is tempting to start tuning. A quicker first step is to check whether it can learn at all. Take just thirty-two training images, switch off every regulariser, and train. A healthy model and pipeline will drive the training loss essentially to zero within a few hundred steps, because, as section one showed, a network can memorise a handful of images easily. If the loss stays stuck, the problem is not generalisation, it is a bug, and no amount of tuning will fix it. In the example the cause is a stray detach that stops any gradient reaching the convolutional layers. Other usual suspects are labels in the wrong order, a missing optimiser step, or a learning rate off by orders of magnitude. The test takes minutes and rules out a whole class of failures. Then look inside the layers. The table shows per-layer gradient norms for a deep network built with sigmoid activations. The gradient reaching the first layer is three times ten to the minus seven, against one tenth at the head: it is vanishing on the way back. The reason shows in the activations: ninety-six percent of the first layer's sigmoid units are saturated, where their derivative is nearly zero.

A single neural score means little on its own. It needs three things beside it: a baseline, ablations, and the spread across seeds. Here every pipeline is run with five seeds on the same batch-split validation folds. The classical baseline, hand features with logistic regression, scores nought point seven one, the same every time because it has no random initialisation. The full CNN averages nought point eight five eight with a standard deviation under a hundredth, a real gain of about fifteen points over the baseline. Then the ablations, each removing exactly one component and keeping everything else fixed. Without augmentation, the CNN drops to nought point eight one six, so augmentation is worth about four points, well beyond the seed noise. Without batch normalisation, it scores nought point eight five, a difference smaller than one standard deviation. Batch norm adds nothing measurable on this task, and the honest report says so rather than keeping it because it is customary. The general rule is to compare differences with the seed spread, not with zero. And remember the seeds all share the same data and splits, so their spread understates the full uncertainty a new dataset would bring.

The evaluation tools from the Machine Learning course apply to neural models unchanged: slice the test set, report counts, check calibration. What is specific to an image model is what tends to shift. The table slices the chosen CNN's test batches. Stations A and B, both represented in training, score nought point eight eight and nought point eight six, with calibration errors under five hundredths. The newly installed station C scores nought point seven one, with dent recall falling to about a half and a calibration error of nought point one two. Dark-finish parts are worse still for dents, nought point four eight, though from only ninety-five images. The causes are physical. Station C has a new lens, so the images look different even though the defects are the same: the input distribution moved and the labels did not. On dark-finish parts, dents do not cast the shadow that the model had learned to rely on. Under both shifts the model becomes overconfident, its probabilities no longer matching its accuracy. Recalibration on new-station data can repair the probabilities, but it cannot restore a cue the model has lost; that needs training images from the new conditions.

The chapter ends by turning evidence into claims, and being exact about which claims the evidence supports. It does support a macro F1 of about nought point eight six on stations A and B, measured on locked test batches and averaged over five seeds, and it supports using the model as a routing aid that sends likely defects to a manual check. It does not support claims about a new station, where performance was measured at nought point seven one. It only weakly supports dent detection on dark-finish parts, based on ninety-five images with recall below a half. It does not support reading a saliency heat map as the reason for a decision: such maps show where the output is sensitive, which is not the same as why the model decided, and the Machine Learning course's cautions about explanations apply. And nothing here supports replacing human inspection. All of that is written down alongside the model: its scope, meaning which stations, finishes and lenses it was evaluated on; the label quality, including the eight percent disagreement; the known failures; and the rule for when to re-check, which is whenever a station, camera or part finish changes.

A convolutional layer slides one small filter across the image and computes the same weighted sum at every position. Here is the computation on a five-by-five grey patch with a bright vertical scratch in its middle column, and a three-by-three filter that is minus one on the left, zero in the centre and plus one on the right. At each position, multiply the filter element by element with the window of pixels under it and add everything up. In the first column of the output, the window's right edge falls on the scratch, so the plus-ones meet bright pixels and the sum is twenty-four. Centred on the scratch, left and right cancel and the output is zero. Just past it, the minus-ones meet the scratch and the sum is minus twenty-four. The filter is a vertical-edge detector, and it fires wherever such an edge occurs. Two assumptions are built in. Locality: each output depends only on a small neighbourhood. And weight sharing: the same nine weights are used everywhere, which says a scratch is a scratch whatever its position. One convention to know: what PyTorch calls convolution is mathematically a cross-correlation, without flipping the filter. For learned filters it makes no difference; for filters copied from a textbook it can.

A real convolutional layer has many filters, and each filter is three-dimensional: it spans every channel of its input. The first layer of our defect CNN takes three colour channels and produces sixteen feature maps, so it has sixteen filters, each three channels by three by three, which is four hundred and thirty-two weights, plus sixteen biases: four hundred and forty-eight parameters. The second layer maps sixteen channels to thirty-two, four thousand six hundred and forty parameters; the third maps thirty-two to sixty-four, eighteen thousand four hundred and ninety-six. With the small linear head, the whole network has twenty-three thousand seven hundred and seventy-nine parameters, which is under a sixteenth of the MLP's first layer on its own. The table also tracks shapes. Padding of one pixel keeps each convolution's output at the same size as its input, and each two-by-two max pool halves the height and width, from sixty-four to thirty-two to sixteen. Meanwhile the number of channels grows, a common pattern: less spatial detail, more kinds of feature. At the end, global average pooling averages each of the sixty-four feature maps to a single number, so the head sees a fixed-length vector whatever the image size.

Three settings control the size of a convolution's output: padding, stride and dilation, and the formula in the table combines them with the filter size. A three-by-three filter with one pixel of padding keeps a sixty-four-pixel input at sixty-four. Without padding the output shrinks to sixty-two, because the filter cannot be centred on the border pixels. A stride of two moves the filter two pixels at a time and halves the output to thirty-two. Dilation spaces the filter's taps apart, so a three-by-three filter with dilation two covers a five-by-five area while keeping nine weights. These settings, together with depth, determine the receptive field: the patch of the input image that a unit in a given layer depends on. Each convolution widens it by the filter size minus one, multiplied by the product of all earlier strides, so pooling and striding make later layers grow it much faster. In our small CNN, a unit after the first convolution sees three pixels, after the second eight, and after the third eighteen. That is a design constraint: a dent wider than eighteen pixels is never seen whole by any single unit of the last convolution, and global pooling can only combine those partial views.

Pooling summarises each small window of a feature map with a single number, most often its maximum. Two-by-two max pooling with a stride of two turns a four-by-four feature map into two-by-two, keeping the strongest response in each quarter: here eight in the top-left window, nothing in two others, and three in the bottom-right. It halves the resolution and adds a little tolerance to position. Now shift the same feature map one pixel to the right. The eight moves within its window, or into the neighbouring one, and the three at the right edge falls off the map entirely. The pooled output becomes zero and eight on the top row and nothing below: a different result for an input that differs by one pixel. This is worth being precise about. A convolution is shift-equivariant: shift the input and its output shifts by the same amount, at least away from the borders. Pooling only makes small shifts within a window invisible. Strides, borders and padding all break exact invariance, so convolutional networks are less translation-invariant than they are often described. The practical consequence is that a defect classifier still needs training images with defects in varied positions.

Stacking more convolutional layers should, in principle, never hurt: the extra layers could simply learn to pass their input through unchanged. In practice very deep plain networks train worse than shallower ones, because passing a signal through unchanged turns out to be hard to learn. Residual connections fix this by changing what each block has to learn. A residual block computes some correction F of x and adds the input back, then applies ReLU. If the block has nothing useful to add, it only needs F of x to be near zero, which is easy. And the skip path gives gradients a direct route back to early layers, past every nonlinearity. Adding requires matching shapes. The block in the figure halves the resolution and doubles the channels, from sixteen channels at thirty-two pixels square to thirty-two channels at sixteen. The input cannot simply be added to that, so the shortcut becomes a projection: a one-by-one convolution with stride two, followed by batch norm. It is cheap. The main path, two three-by-three convolutions with batch norm, has thirteen thousand nine hundred and fifty-two parameters; the projection only five hundred and seventy-six. The sum happens before the final ReLU.

Batch normalisation standardises each channel so that later layers see inputs of a stable scale, and it behaves differently in training and evaluation. Here it is on a single channel with a batch of four values: two, four, six and eight. In training mode it uses the batch's own statistics, a mean of five and a variance of five, and the output is minus one point three four, minus nought point four five, nought point four five and one point three four: zero mean and unit variance. Learned scale and shift parameters then let the network undo that if it helps; here they are at their defaults. At the same time, it updates running statistics, moving them ten percent of the way toward this batch: the running mean goes from zero to a half, the running variance from one to one point five seven. In evaluation mode it uses those running statistics instead of the batch's. Applied to the very same batch, the output is now one point two up to six. That is not a bug: the running statistics simply need many training steps to settle. The consequences are worth remembering. Forgetting eval lets validation batches change the statistics. Tiny batches give noisy statistics. And the running statistics are buffers, saved with the model.

Batch norm and layer norm compute the same thing, subtract a mean and divide by a standard deviation, but over different axes, and that difference changes their behaviour completely. Take a tiny tensor of two examples with three features each: one, two, three, and four, six, eight. Batch normalisation works per feature, across the examples in the batch. Each feature column has just the two values, so each becomes minus one and plus one, and both rows come out as all minus ones and all plus ones. What is left is only which example was larger. Layer normalisation works per example, across its own features. Both rows have values evenly spaced around their own mean, so both become minus one point two two, zero, one point two two. The fact that the second example was twice as large is gone; the pattern within each example is kept. Layer norm has two practical advantages: it does not depend on the batch at all, so batch size does not matter, and it behaves identically in training and evaluation, with no running statistics to manage. That makes it the standard in sequence models and transformers. Batch norm remains common in CNNs trained with large batches. Where the normalisation sits relative to the residual addition matters as well.

A last comparison corrects a common intuition: fewer parameters does not mean less computation. The MLP has three hundred and ninety-three thousand parameters and does about the same number of multiply-adds per image, because each weight is used exactly once. The CNN has under twenty-four thousand parameters, yet does about eleven point two million multiply-adds per image, because every filter weight is reused at every position of its feature map. The per-layer table shows where that arithmetic goes: the second and third convolutions account for about eighty-four percent of it, since they apply many channels at fairly high resolution. Memory follows the same pattern: the activations that must be kept for backward scale with resolution times channels, which chapter twelve measures. Convolution is not only for images. The workshop's sensor history is a sequence of four sensor readings over a hundred and twenty time steps. A one-dimensional convolution with sixteen filters of length five has three hundred and thirty-six parameters and produces a hundred and sixteen output steps. The assumptions are the same, now in time: patterns are local and look the same wherever they occur. One caution carries into the next chapter: an ordinary kernel centred on a time step also sees the future within its window.

Ordered data arrives in two forms, and this chapter uses both. Text arrives as tokens. Short notes written by the inspectors, such as scratch on lid, are split into tokens, and a vocabulary maps each token to an integer id: scratch is two, on is four, lid is five. A word the vocabulary has never seen, like hinge here, maps to a reserved unknown id. The ids themselves are just labels, with no meaningful size or order, so the network converts each into a vector using an embedding table: a matrix with one learned row per id, here four numbers long. Embedding a token is nothing more than looking up its row, and those rows are trained like any other weights, so tokens used in similar ways drift toward similar vectors. The padding id gets a row fixed at zero that is never updated. The second form is continuous: the workshop's sensor history is already numbers, four sensor readings at each of a hundred and twenty time steps, so it needs no lookup, only scaling, with means and spreads computed from the training months. And the same rule as every chapter applies to the vocabulary: it is learned state, built from training text only.

For ordered data, the most important part of the contract is which steps are visible when each prediction is made, and the answer depends on the task. Sequence classification gives one label to a complete sequence: a finished inspector's note, labelled as a dent report or not. Every word exists by the time we predict, so the model may use all of them, in any direction. Causal forecasting is the opposite: from the sensor history up to time t, predict the reading at t plus one. The future has not happened yet, so it must never be visible, in training any more than at prediction time. Tagging gives one output per step, and may use later steps only if the whole input really is available when predictions are made. Generation produces a sequence one step at a time, left to right, so each step sees only what came before. For the sensor task, the boundaries come straight from the Machine Learning course. Split by time, training on earlier months and testing on later ones. Split by machine as well if the claim is about machines the model has never seen. Training windows must not straddle the split. And readings that arrive late are not available at prediction time, even if they are timestamped earlier.

An autoregressive objective turns a single sequence into many training examples. At every position, the model predicts the next token. In practice that is done by shifting: the inputs are the sequence without its last token, and the targets are the sequence without its first. So from the beginning-of-sequence marker, predict scratch; from scratch, predict on; from on, predict lid; and from lid, predict the end marker. Every position trains at once, which is why this objective is so data-efficient, but it only makes sense if the prediction at position t depends on inputs up to t and no further. A recurrent network satisfies that by construction; chapter nine shows how transformers enforce it with a mask. Our fragment was padded to six tokens, so the last target is padding, and that position must not count. The table shows the model's probability for each true target and the loss, minus its logarithm: nought point nine one six, nought point six nine three, one point two zero four and nought point five one one. Predicting padding after the end marker is trivially easy, a loss of two hundredths. Averaged over the four valid positions, the loss is nought point eight three one. Include the padding and it drops to nought point six six nine, a better number for a meaningless reason.

A recurrent network processes a sequence one step at a time and carries a hidden state forward, a summary of everything it has seen so far. At each step it combines the previous state with the new input using the same weights, then applies a nonlinearity. Here is the smallest possible version, with a single hidden unit, a recurrent weight of nought point eight, an input weight of one and no bias, run on four sensor readings starting from a state of zero. The first reading, nought point five, gives a state of nought point four six two. The second, one point zero, adds to the remembered state, and the pre-activation of one point three seven becomes nought point eight seven nine. The third reading is negative, minus a half, and pulls the state down sharply, but the memory of the previous step keeps it positive, at nought point two. The fourth gives nought point three four five. Unrolled in time, the network looks like a deep stack of layers, one per step, all sharing their weights. That sharing is what lets one model handle sequences of any length, with a parameter count that does not grow with time. The cost is that everything the model keeps about the past must fit into that one state vector.

Training a recurrent network means backpropagating through the unrolled sequence, which is called backpropagation through time. Because the same weights are applied at every step, the gradient flowing back to an earlier step is multiplied by a local factor at each step it crosses, and for the simple network that factor is the recurrent weight times the derivative of tanh. The plot shows what a product of many such factors does. If the typical factor is nought point seven, then twenty steps back the gradient is less than one thousandth of its original size, so an early reading has almost no influence on learning. If the factor is one point one, twenty steps back it is nearly seven times larger, and longer sequences blow up. That is why plain recurrent networks struggle with dependencies more than a few dozen steps long. Long sensor histories also cost memory, since every step's activations are stored for backward. The standard compromise is truncated backpropagation through time: process the history in chunks of, say, thirty-two steps, carry the hidden state forward from chunk to chunk, but detach it at each boundary. The state still remembers, but gradients reach back at most thirty-two steps, a limit you choose and state. Clipping handles the exploding case.

Long short-term memory networks attack the vanishing-gradient problem by changing how the state is updated. Alongside the hidden state they keep a separate cell state, and three gates, each a sigmoid between zero and one, decide what happens to it. Here is one step traced from a previous cell value of a half, with gate pre-activations chosen for illustration. The forget gate is the sigmoid of two, nought point eight eight one, so the cell keeps eighty-eight percent of its old value. The input gate is the sigmoid of zero, a half, and it scales a candidate value, the tanh of one, nought point seven six two. The new cell is the kept part plus the admitted part: nought point eight two one. The output gate, nought point seven three one, decides how much of the cell to expose, and the hidden state is that gate times the tanh of the cell, nought point four nine four. The key is that the cell is updated by addition rather than by repeated multiplication through a nonlinearity, so when the forget gate is near one, both the memory and its gradient pass through many steps largely intact. A GRU is a lighter variant with two gates and no separate cell. Both cost several times a plain RNN's weights.

A bidirectional recurrent network runs two passes over a sequence, one forward and one backward, and combines their states at each step. That means every step's output depends on the steps after it as well as before. Whether that is allowed is purely a question of the visibility contract. For classifying a finished inspector's note, it is fine and usually helpful, because every word exists when the prediction is made. For forecasting the next sensor reading, it is a leak: the backward pass has read the future, and a model trained that way will score brilliantly in validation and be impossible to deploy. The same applies to flagging a fault as it happens, since later readings are not yet available. Recurrent state can leak in more practical ways too. If the hidden state is carried from batch to batch, it must be carried within one machine's stream; letting machine A's state flow into machine B's sequence mixes unrelated histories. Reset it at the start of every independent sequence. And padding causes trouble here as well: in a padded batch, the RNN keeps updating its state through the padding steps. Packing the sequences makes it stop at each one's true length, so the final state is the real one.

Sequence models that generate their own future, a forecast several steps ahead or a continued note, are usually trained with teacher forcing: at each training step, the model is fed the true previous value, not its own earlier prediction. That makes training fast and stable. But at prediction time the true future values do not exist, so the model has to feed its own predictions back in, and any error it makes becomes part of its next input. The plot shows the consequence for the sensor forecast. Measured one step at a time with the true history supplied, the error is about nought point eight degrees at every horizon. Run free, feeding its own predictions back, the errors compound, reaching about four degrees twelve steps ahead. A one-step validation score badly overstates a twelve-step forecast. So the evaluation has to imitate deployment. Train on January to June, choose the checkpoint and settings on July, and test once on August, running the model free at the horizons the decision actually needs. Never shuffle windows across that time cut. And note the remaining limit: dependencies longer than the truncation window, or than the state can hold, are simply lost, which is the problem attention addresses next.

Attention answers a simple question for every token: which other tokens should I draw information from, and how much? Each token is projected three ways. Its query describes what it is looking for, its key describes what it offers, and its value is the information it passes on if chosen. A query is compared with every key by a dot product, divided by the square root of the key width, and a softmax turns those scores into weights that sum to one. The output is the weighted average of the values. Here is the chapter's worked trace, the inspector note dent on lid, with keys four wide, so we divide by two. The query for lid scores one, a half and one against dent, on and lid. The softmax gives weights of nought point three eight four, nought point two three three and nought point three eight four. Multiplying each by its value and adding gives an output of one point one five one, one point nought. Two things change from recurrence. Every pair of tokens is compared directly, however far apart they are, and because no state is carried along, every query can be computed at once, as a single matrix multiply.

The score function decides how a query is compared with a key, and two forms are standard. Additive attention, from the first recurrent translation models, runs a small network on every pair: it projects the query and the key, adds them, applies a tanh and reads off a score. It allows the query and key to have different widths, at the cost of extra parameters. Scaled dot-product attention simply takes the dot product of query and key and divides by the square root of their width. It has no parameters of its own, and every pair is scored in one matrix multiply, which is why it won. The division matters. If query and key entries have unit variance, their dot product has variance equal to the width, so raw scores grow as the model widens. Large scores push the softmax towards one-hot, where almost all the weight sits on one key and the gradients through the other keys nearly vanish. The plot measures this over two hundred random draws with eight keys. Unscaled, the largest weight averages nought point eight eight at width sixty-four and nought point nine seven at five hundred and twelve. Scaled, it stays near nought point three six at every width, well above uniform attention's one eighth.

Masks decide which keys a query may see, and they belong before the softmax. A masked score is set to minus infinity, so its exponential is exactly zero and the remaining weights still sum to one. The worked trace uses two masks at once. The padding mask removes the PAD key for every query. The causal mask stops each query from seeing keys after its own position, which is what a model predicting the next token needs. Now dent can only see itself, so its weight is one. On splits its attention, nought point three seven eight on dent and nought point six two two on itself. Lid is unchanged, because there was no later real token for it to lose. Two shortcuts break this. Setting weights to zero after the softmax leaves rows that no longer sum to one, and setting a score to zero rather than minus infinity still gives that key positive weight. The sharper failure is a row where every key is masked, such as an empty note in the batch. The softmax then computes nought over nought, which is not a number, and one NaN spreads through the next multiply into the loss. Drop empty sequences, keep one slot that is always valid, or zero those outputs explicitly.

Self-attention and cross-attention run exactly the same computation. What differs is where the queries, keys and values come from. In self-attention all three come from one sequence. A twelve-token inspector note attends over itself, the weights form a twelve by twelve grid for each example, and each token's output mixes in context from the rest of the note. In cross-attention the queries come from one sequence and the keys and values from another. Here the note's twelve tokens attend over forty-nine feature vectors taken from a seven by seven grid of the defect image's patches. The weights are now twelve by forty-nine, and the output has the query's length, twelve tokens, each now carrying information drawn from the image. The keys and values must have the same length as each other, but the queries need not match it. A useful habit is to read every score tensor as batch, query length, key length. The padding mask follows the keys, so in self-attention it marks the note's padding, and in cross-attention it marks any missing patches. In PyTorch it is literally the same module: pass the note three times for self-attention, or the note once and the patches twice for cross-attention.

In practice attention runs as several heads side by side. With a model width of sixty-four and eight heads, each projection is reshaped from batch, tokens, sixty-four into batch, eight heads, tokens, eight. Each head computes its own grid of weights, so one head can follow the defect word while another follows the location. The head outputs are concatenated back to width sixty-four and mixed by an output projection. Because each head is narrow, the total cost is about the same as one full-width head. Attention also has a blind spot: it ignores order. Take the worked note and reverse it, lid on dent, without any position information. Every token produces exactly the output it produced before. Dent still gives one point three two, nought point eight, and lid still gives one point one five, one. Self-attention is permutation equivariant: reorder the inputs and the outputs reorder the same way, nothing more. For text or sensor readings that is wrong, so position must be added. Absolute schemes add a learned or sinusoidal vector for each index. Relative schemes add a bias to each score based on the distance between the two positions. Rotary schemes rotate queries and keys by their index. Only genuine sets should go without.

Comparing every token with every other token is what makes attention powerful, and it is also what makes it expensive. The score tensor has one entry for every pair of positions in every head, so its memory and compute grow with the square of the sequence length. For one layer in thirty-two bit floats, with a batch of thirty-two and eight heads, the scores take about one gigabyte at a length of one thousand and twenty-four, and seventeen gigabytes at four thousand and ninety-six, while the token activations themselves take about a quarter of a gigabyte. Doubling the length quadruples the score memory. Fused attention kernels avoid storing the full grid, but they still do work proportional to the square of the length. The weights are also easy to over-read. A high weight on a token whose value vector is small contributes little to the output. Several heads and layers are mixed together afterwards, and the residual connection carries information around attention entirely. So a weight shows where a query looked, not what caused the prediction. If you want to claim a token mattered, test it: remove or replace that token, score the example again, and measure the change.

A transformer is a stack of identical blocks, and each block does two things. First an attention sublayer mixes information between positions. Then a small feedforward network transforms each token on its own, here widening its sixty-four features to two hundred and fifty-six and back. Each sublayer is wrapped in a residual connection, so the block adds a correction to its input rather than replacing it, and in the pre-norm arrangement shown here a layer normalisation sits before each sublayer, rescaling each token's sixty-four features. The input and output shapes are the same, batch by tokens by sixty-four, which is what lets blocks stack. Counting parameters makes the balance clear. The four attention projections, for queries, keys, values and output, each have sixty-four by sixty-four weights plus a bias, sixteen thousand six hundred and forty in all. The feedforward network has thirty-three thousand and eighty-eight. The two layer norms add two hundred and fifty-six, for a block total of forty-nine thousand nine hundred and eighty-four, two thirds of it in the feedforward part. The residual path is what lets gradients reach the earliest blocks, the same idea as the residual blocks of chapter six, and putting the norm first keeps deep stacks stable.

Without position information, a stack of transformer blocks treats a note as a set of tokens, as we saw when reversing dent on lid changed nothing. Order has to be put in on purpose. The original transformer adds a fixed sinusoidal vector to each token's embedding. Each pair of dimensions is a sine and cosine at its own frequency. The lowest dimensions turn quickly, repeating every six point three positions, while higher ones turn slowly, every twenty positions at the fourth pair and every sixty-three at the eighth. Read together, the sixty-four dimensions give every position a distinct pattern, and nearby positions get similar ones. There are four common schemes. Learned absolute embeddings train one vector per index, so a position beyond the training length simply has no vector. Sinusoidal codes are defined at any index, but models rarely use them reliably past what they were trained on. Relative schemes add a bias to each attention score based on the distance between the two positions. Rotary schemes rotate queries and keys by their index, so their dot product depends only on the offset between them. Everything else in the block treats positions identically, so the position scheme is the only thing that distinguishes dent on lid from lid on dent.

The same transformer block can be arranged in three ways, and the difference is what each position is allowed to see. That follows directly from the task. An encoder-only model uses bidirectional self-attention, so every token sees every other. It fits when the whole input exists at prediction time and the output is a label or a tag per token, such as classifying a finished inspector note as ok, scratch or dent. A decoder-only model uses causal self-attention, so each token sees only itself and what came before. It fits when the output is a sequence that is continued one token at a time, such as completing a note from its first few words. An encoder-decoder model combines the two. The encoder reads the input with bidirectional attention, the decoder writes the output with causal attention, and between them, cross-attention lets every decoder token read the encoder's states. It fits when one sequence is mapped to a different one, such as turning a sensor history of a hundred and twenty steps into a short written fault summary. These are architectural choices about visibility. They do not, on their own, decide what the model is trained to predict. That is the objective, and it comes two sections from now.

A visibility mask is a grid of permissions, one row for each query and one column for each key. Comparing two of them on the same padded note, scratch on lid edge plus one padding slot, shows exactly what each one hides. With a bidirectional mask and padding, every real token can see all four real tokens, sixteen visible pairs, and only the padding column is hidden. That is what an encoder reading a finished note wants. Add the causal mask and query number i can only see keys one up to i, so the whole upper triangle disappears. The visible pairs fall from sixteen to ten, one plus two plus three plus four. Scratch now sees only itself, while edge, the last token, still sees the whole note. That is right for a decoder, because when it is generating, the later tokens do not exist yet. Cross-attention has its own rule. Every decoder token may look at every encoder position, because the input sequence is complete before decoding starts, and only the encoder's padding is masked. In PyTorch, the causal grid is the upper triangle above the diagonal, built with triu and a diagonal offset of one, where true means hidden.

A transformer's mask decides what each position may see. Its objective decides which positions are scored, and against what target. These are separate choices, and the common objectives pair them in particular ways. Next-token prediction uses the inputs shifted by one as targets: from the tokens up to position t, predict token t plus one. Every position carries a loss. For the note scratch on lid edge, with illustrative probabilities for each correct next token, the losses are one point two, nought point five one, nought point nine two and nought point six nine, a mean cross-entropy of nought point eight three. This objective needs the causal mask, because without it each position could simply read its own target from the next slot. Masked-token prediction hides some tokens, here replacing on with a mask token, and scores only those positions. The model gives on a probability of nought point seven, a loss of nought point three six, and the other positions contribute nothing. Because the hidden token is replaced in the input, this objective can use a bidirectional mask, and the prediction draws on context from both sides. Mixing them up fails in instructive ways. Next-token training without the causal mask is leakage, and its training loss falls towards zero.

A causal decoder is fast to train and slow to use, and both facts come from the causal mask. During training, the whole true note goes in at once, beginning-of-sequence, scratch, on, lid. The causal mask stops each position seeing the token it has to predict, so the model produces all four next-token predictions, and all four losses, from a single forward pass. The work is parallel over both the batch and the positions, which is the big practical advantage over a recurrent network. Generation cannot do that. Each new token depends on the token chosen just before it, so a four-token note needs four forward passes, and each pass uses only the logits at the last position. The inputs are now the model's own choices rather than the true note. That gap is teacher forcing again, from chapter seven. During training the model never conditions on its own mistakes, but during generation an early wrong token becomes part of the context for every later one. The table sets the two modes side by side. One last cost is visible in the loop: each pass reads the whole prefix again, recomputing keys and values for tokens it has already processed.
