Removing that repeated work is what the next section's cache is for.

Generation repeats work. At every step the model recomputes keys and values for tokens it has already processed, even though those never change. A key-value cache stores them, so each step computes keys and values for the new token only. Generating a thousand and twenty-four tokens then takes a thousand and twenty-four key and value projections per layer, instead of over half a million. The cache does not make long contexts free. The new token's query still attends over every cached key, so the work per step grows with the context, and the cache itself has to be held in memory. For a six-layer decoder with width five hundred and twelve in sixteen-bit floats, keys and values take twelve point three kilobytes per token. One sequence of four thousand and ninety-six tokens needs fifty megabytes, and a batch of thirty-two needs one point six gigabytes. In serving, that memory, not the arithmetic, is often the limit on batch size and context length. Once the logits are computed, a decoding rule picks the next token. Greedy decoding takes the most likely token, deterministic but often repetitive. Temperature, top-k and top-p sampling draw from a sharpened or truncated distribution. Beam search keeps the best few partial sequences, at several times the compute.

Pretraining loss measures how well a model predicts text. That is useful, but it is not the same as the text being true, or a task being solved. These illustrative checkpoints come from a model pretrained on workshop notes. All the numbers are validation evidence. The validation next-token loss falls steadily from three point nine to one point nine five, and perplexity, which is e raised to the loss, falls from about forty-nine to seven. Alongside it, the model is asked two hundred part-number questions with answers that can be checked. Its accuracy climbs to fifty percent by eight thousand steps, and then stalls at fifty-one, even though the loss keeps improving for another twenty-four thousand steps. The two measure different things. Next-token loss rewards continuations that are plausible, whether or not they are correct. A rare fact, like one part number, carries very little weight in a loss averaged over every token. And a fluent but wrong answer can score a low loss. So if a task matters, measure the task: a held-out set with answers that can be checked, errors broken down by type rather than one average, and a working assumption that any fact the model generates is a claim to verify, not a result.

Transfer learning reuses an encoder trained on one task, the source, as the starting point for another, the target. It helps exactly as far as the two tasks share what the target needs. These learning curves are validation evidence on the workshop defect task, split by production batch. The small convolutional network from scratch needs data: it reaches nought point five two with six hundred labelled images and nought point eight seven with all two thousand four hundred. An encoder pretrained on a large set of general photographs, then fine-tuned, reaches nought point eight five with only six hundred images, and nought point nine three at the full budget. Its source objective, naming objects, rewarded features for edges, texture and lighting, which defect detection needs. The third curve starts from an encoder trained on clean computer renders of the parts. It is ahead at a hundred and fifty images, then stalls at nought point eight four, below the model trained from scratch. That is negative transfer. The renders share the parts' shape, but contain no scratches, dents or surface texture, so their features are a poor starting point. Before transferring, ask what the source objective rewarded, how close its images are to the target camera, and whether transfer still wins at the full labelled budget.

The cheapest way to adapt a pretrained network is to keep its body frozen and train only a new head on top of its features. The pretrained ResNet eighteen ends in a head that predicts a thousand source classes. For the workshop task that head is replaced with a linear layer from the five hundred and twelve features to three defect classes, one thousand five hundred and thirty-nine trainable parameters. The body's eleven point two million weights stay fixed. Training only that layer is called a linear probe. With six hundred labelled images, it reaches a validation macro F one of nought point seven four. A small two-layer head adds sixty-six thousand parameters and reaches nought point seven six. Unfreezing the last stage of the body as well, about eight point four million parameters, reaches nought point eight three. Fine-tuning everything reaches nought point eight five. A probe score has a clear meaning: it measures what the frozen features already separate, with no chance for the body to adapt. It is cheap, fast, and hard to overfit with few labels, which makes it the right first baseline for any transfer decision. The code is short: switch off gradients for every parameter, then assign a new final layer, whose parameters are trainable by default.

Fine-tuning goes further than a probe: it updates the pretrained body as well as the new head. How fast each layer is allowed to move decides whether the pretrained features are refined or overwritten. These three validation curves all start from the same pretrained body, with six hundred labelled images. The frozen body with a linear probe climbs quickly and settles at nought point seven four. A single learning rate of one in a thousand for every layer is the common mistake. Large updates driven by a random new head wreck the pretrained features in the first epoch, the score drops to about a half, and it recovers only to nought point six seven. Per-layer learning rates reach nought point eight five, the best of the three. The reasoning follows the network's depth. Early layers hold generic edges and textures that transfer well, so they change least, or stay frozen. Later layers hold more source-specific features, so they are allowed to move more. The new head starts from random weights and gets the largest rate. In PyTorch this is a list of parameter groups, each with its own rate. Freezing more layers trains faster and stores fewer gradients. Full fine-tuning can win when labels are plentiful, but with few labels it overfits sooner.

Freezing a network by switching off gradients stops its weights from being updated by the optimiser. It does not stop batch normalisation from changing. In training mode, every batch norm layer keeps updating its running mean and variance from the batches it sees, whatever requires grad says. Here is one channel. The source data left its running mean at zero. Every target batch has a mean of nought point six, and the momentum is nought point one. After one batch the running mean is nought point nought six. After ten it is nought point three nine, and after fifty it is nought point five nine seven, almost entirely the target's statistics. The scale parameter gamma never moved and has no gradient, yet the layer now normalises differently, so the body you thought was frozen is not the body you probed. Two other pieces of state behave the same way. Dropout is still active in training mode, and optimiser state exists only for the parameters you passed in. The fix is to put the batch norm modules back into evaluation mode after calling train on the model. Or adapt the statistics deliberately, and record that choice. Either way, check by comparing the named buffers before and after an epoch.

Self-supervised learning makes its training targets from the data itself, so an encoder can be pretrained on the workshop's forty thousand unlabelled archive images before any inspector labels them. Three signals are common. A masked signal hides patches of an image, or tokens of a note, and asks the model to rebuild them. A predictive signal asks it to forecast what comes next, such as the next window of sensor readings. A contrastive signal makes two augmented views of the same image and trains the encoder to map them close together and away from other images. The table traces the contrastive InfoNCE loss for one anchor with a temperature of nought point one. The positive view has a cosine similarity of nought point six, which becomes four hundred and three after dividing by the temperature and exponentiating. One negative, a similar dent from another image, scores nought point five and takes a quarter of the mass. The positive's share is nought point seven two, and the loss is minus its log, nought point three three. Hard negatives like that one dominate the loss. In a batch, each row's positive is on the diagonal and every other image is a negative. Not every method needs negatives: designs with a predictor and a stop-gradient can avoid collapse without them.

A contrastive encoder learns to ignore whatever differs between the two views of a positive pair. So the views must change only what the downstream task does not care about. For defect images that rules out some familiar augmentations. Horizontal flips and small rotations keep a two-pixel scratch, so they are safe. A random crop of thirty percent of the image often cuts the scratch out entirely, so the two views no longer share the defect, and the encoder is rewarded for matching a scratched view to a clean one. A strong blur erases fine scratches and teaches the encoder that scratches do not matter, the opposite of what inspection needs. Colour jitter keeps scratches, but it can hide discolouring, so check it per defect class. Two other failures come from the signal itself. False negatives arise when two images of very similar dents land in one batch: the loss pushes them apart even though they belong together. Group the batches, or drop near-duplicates from each other's negatives. Collapse is the extreme case: if every image maps to the same point, all views agree trivially. A cheap check is the standard deviation of the embeddings across a batch. For spread-out unit vectors in a hundred and twenty-eight dimensions it sits near nought point nought nine; falling towards zero means collapse.

Self-supervised pretraining uses no labels, so it is tempting to pretrain on every image available, including the test images. But an encoder that has seen the test images has already learned their particular lighting, backgrounds and defects, and that inflates the test score. In this example the camera archive used for pretraining held three hundred and ten of the four hundred and eighty test images. These are final-test results for one encoder and head. On all four hundred and eighty images the linear probe scores nought point eight nine and the fine-tuned model nought point nine one. On the hundred and seventy images that were never in the archive, they score nought point seven eight and nought point eight four. The probe gains most from contamination, eleven points, because it relies entirely on the pretrained features. Keeping it clean means removing the test batches from the pretraining pool before pretraining, by batch identifier and image hash, and checking for near-duplicates, such as the same part photographed twice, not just identical files. The clean score is the result to report. Report both protocols on the same splits. A linear probe shows what the frozen features already separate. A fine-tune shows how far the body can adapt, and needs its parameter groups, rates and budget stated.

A pretrained checkpoint is a dependency like any other, and it brings assumptions with it. Record where it came from before you build on it. That means the source data, what it contained, when it was collected and under what licence. The objective it was trained with, supervised labels or a particular self-supervised signal. The preprocessing it expects, the input size and the normalisation mean and standard deviation, since feeding it differently scaled images quietly degrades every feature. The exact weights file, by hash. An overlap check against your test batches. And the terms that say whether it may be used for this purpose at all. With that recorded, choose the smallest adaptation the evidence supports. With about a hundred and fifty labels and a close source, start with a linear probe. With about six hundred, train the last stage and the head, and go further only if per-layer rates beat that on validation. With all two thousand four hundred, compare full fine-tuning against training from scratch on the same split, because transfer is no longer guaranteed to win. If the source is unclear or its licence does not allow this use, train from scratch until that is resolved. Finally, record whether the batch norm statistics were frozen or adapted, because that changes the model too.

An autoencoder learns to reproduce its input after squeezing it through a narrow code. It needs no labels, because the input is its own target. For a sensor window of a hundred and twenty steps across four sensors, the encoder maps four hundred and eighty numbers down to sixteen, the bottleneck, and the decoder maps those sixteen back to four hundred and eighty, reshaped into the original window. The loss is the mean squared difference between the window and its reconstruction. The smallest possible case makes the mechanics visible: three channel means, a one-number code, and three outputs, with the encoder and decoder sharing one unit direction, nought point six, nought, nought point eight. The input is nought point nine, nought point two, nought point four. Encoding takes the dot product, giving a code of nought point eight six. Decoding multiplies the direction by that code, giving nought point five one six, nought, nought point six eight eight. The errors are nought point three eight, nought point two and minus nought point two nine, and the mean squared loss is nought point nought nine. The middle channel is lost entirely, because the direction gives it no weight. That is what a bottleneck forces. Sixteen numbers cannot hold every detail of four hundred and eighty, so training keeps whatever lowers the average loss the most.

There is a precise link between autoencoders and principal component analysis. With linear layers, squared error and centred data, the best possible autoencoder code spans the same subspace as the top principal components. The plot shows it on eighty centred two-dimensional points. PCA's first direction is nought point eight three three, nought point five five three. A linear autoencoder with a one-number code, trained by ordinary gradient descent, ends up pointing the same way, within two hundredths of a degree, and the reconstruction errors match exactly at nought point nought three six nine. The qualifications matter as much as the match. The autoencoder finds the same subspace, not the same basis. Its encoder weights end with a length of one point seven one and its decoder with nought point five nine. Only their product is pinned down, at one, so any rescaling between the two fits equally well. With more than one code dimension, the learned directions can be any mixture of the principal components, neither orthogonal nor ordered by variance. And once you add a nonlinearity, a different loss, or uncentred data, the equivalence no longer holds. So for a linear autoencoder, PCA is the baseline to beat. It has a closed form and needs no training at all.

An autoencoder whose code is as wide as its input, or wider, has an easy way out. It can learn something close to the identity, copy the input straight through, and reach near-perfect reconstruction without learning anything useful about the data. These illustrative validation numbers show it on sensor windows. An undercomplete model with a sixteen-number code reconstructs with an error of nought point nought one eight, and a linear probe on its code predicts the fault label with a macro F one of nought point seven one. An overcomplete model with nine hundred and sixty code units and no constraint reconstructs almost perfectly, nought point nought nought nought three, but its code scores only nought point five five. The best reconstruction gives the worst code. Three ideas make reconstruction non-trivial. A bottleneck gives the code fewer numbers than the input. A sparsity penalty on the code's magnitude lets the code be wide but keeps few units active at once, and here reaches nought point seven three. Denoising corrupts the input with noise but keeps the clean window as the target, so copying the input is no longer enough. The model has to learn the structure that lets it remove the noise, and it scores best, at nought point seven six. The noise goes on the input only, never on the target.

Reconstruction loss rewards whatever gets most of the pixels right. The task you actually care about may depend on only a few of them. This illustrative sweep trains autoencoders on the defect images, widening the code from eight numbers to five hundred and twelve, and records two kinds of validation evidence. The reconstruction error keeps falling the whole way, from nought point nought four one to nought point nought nought one. A linear probe on the code, predicting the defect class, peaks at nought point seven two at a width of sixty-four and then falls to nought point five eight. If you picked the width by reconstruction quality, you would pick the worst code for the task. The arithmetic of a scratch shows why. A scratch two pixels wide and thirty long covers sixty of the four thousand and ninety-six pixels in a sixty-four by sixty-four image, under one and a half percent. If the decoder misses it completely, with an error of a half on every scratch pixel, the mean squared error rises by only nought point nought nought three seven. Background, lighting and surface texture dominate the loss instead. So evaluate the code on the task it is meant to serve: choose widths and variants by a probe on labelled validation data, not by reconstruction.

Train an autoencoder only on normal images and it learns to reconstruct them well, so a high reconstruction error suggests the input is unusual. That makes reconstruction error a popular anomaly score. These are validation results on four hundred normal images, sixty defects, and twenty blank frames produced by a camera fault. The threshold is set at the ninety-ninth percentile of the normal images' error, about thirty-two thousandths. By construction, one percent of normal images are flagged. Two thirds of the defects are flagged, so a third of them pass as normal. And not one of the blank frames is flagged. The blank frames are the most anomalous inputs here, yet they have the lowest errors of all. A uniform image is simply easy to reconstruct. The score measures how reconstructable an input is, not how typical it is, and a model can reconstruct an anomalous input very well. So use it carefully. Set the threshold on normal validation data only, never on the test set, and report what fraction of known defects it misses. Pair it with simple checks that catch the easy failures, such as image brightness or variance, which would flag a blank frame immediately. Treat a low score as an absence of evidence, not as a clean bill of health.

Every autoencoder in this chapter so far maps each input to a single point, its code z. A probabilistic latent model maps each input to a distribution over codes instead, and that small change has large consequences. In a deterministic autoencoder the encoder outputs the code directly, and the loss is reconstruction alone. Codes can end up anywhere in the latent space, so the gaps between them mean nothing, and there is no defined way to sample a new input: a random code may decode to nonsense. A variational autoencoder, in outline, has an encoder that outputs a mean and a log variance for each code dimension. The code is sampled as the mean plus the standard deviation times standard normal noise, which keeps the sampling step differentiable. The loss adds a second term, a KL divergence, which pulls each input's code distribution towards a simple prior, usually a standard normal. Because codes are packed around that prior, decoding a code drawn from the prior produces a plausible new input, so the model can generate. This course stops at that orientation. The full objective, the evidence lower bound, and the wider family of generative models belong to a specialist course. What matters here is recognising which kind of latent a model has, and what it does and does not let you do.

Training memory comes in two parts. One is fixed by the model and the optimiser, the same whatever the batch. The other grows with every example in the batch and with the size of each input. Take the fine-tuned ResNet eighteen from chapter ten, with eleven point one eight million parameters, trained with AdamW in thirty-two-bit floats. The weights take four bytes each, about four hundredths of a gigabyte. The gradients take the same again. Adam keeps two running averages per parameter, another nine hundredths. That is sixteen bytes per parameter, nought point one eight gigabytes in all, at any batch size. The second part is the activations that forward keeps for backward. Counting only the convolution and batch norm outputs at two hundred and twenty-four pixels gives an estimate of twenty point seven megabytes per image: one point three two gigabytes at a batch of sixty-four, and two point six five at a hundred and twenty-eight. For this model the activations outweigh everything else seven to one. Treat that as an estimate, then measure. It leaves out the ReLU outputs, convolution workspaces and the allocator's caching. The measured peak at a batch of sixty-four is three point nine gigabytes, more than twice the estimate. Reset the peak counter, run one full step, and read it back.

Sixteen-bit formats halve the memory of activations and speed up the matrix units on modern accelerators, but each one fails on different numbers. The table rounds the same values into each format. A small gradient of ten to the minus eight underflows to zero in fp16, whose smallest number is about six times ten to the minus eight. Bf16 keeps it, because it has the same exponent range as fp32. Multiply that gradient by a loss scale of sixty-five thousand five hundred and thirty-six first, and it survives in fp16 as about six point five five times ten to the minus four. One plus one ten-thousandth rounds back to one in both formats, so any update smaller than the spacing near a weight's value simply vanishes. And an activation of seventy thousand overflows fp16 to infinity, while bf16 rounds it to seventy thousand one hundred and forty-four. So fp16 has finer steps but a small range, and needs loss scaling. Bf16 has fp32's range but coarser steps, and usually needs no scaler. Autocast runs matrix multiplies and convolutions in low precision while keeping reductions in fp32, and the optimiser's master weights stay in fp32 so small updates still accumulate. Even then, a precision change is a change to the model's numerics, so it needs a quality check as well as a speed measurement.

When a large batch does not fit in memory, gradient accumulation runs several small batches, adds up their gradients, and steps once. It reproduces the gradient of the mean loss exactly, provided each microbatch's loss is divided by the number of microbatches. Four backward passes on sixteen examples then add up to the gradient of a batch of sixty-four, while activation memory is that of sixteen. What it does not reproduce is any layer that looks across the batch. Batch normalisation is the common one. Over the full sixty-four examples, this channel has a mean of nought point four five five and a standard deviation of nought point three six. The four microbatches see means of nought point eight five, nought point three nine, nought point one nine and nought point three nine. These batches were drawn in station order, so each microbatch holds images from one station, and each one is normalised with its own statistics. The network computes a different function than it would with a true batch of sixty-four, and the running statistics it stores for evaluation differ too. Other batch-dependent losses change in the same way: a contrastive loss gets fifteen negatives per anchor instead of sixty-three. Shuffle the data, switch to group normalisation, or synchronise batch norm statistics across microbatches or devices.

Activation checkpointing trades compute for memory. In the forward pass it keeps only some activations, typically the input to each block, and throws the rest away. During backward it runs each block's forward again to rebuild the activations it needs, then computes the gradients. Take a stack of twelve transformer blocks, where each block keeps nought point four gigabytes of internals for backward and takes an input of nought point nought five gigabytes. Storing everything takes twelve times nought point four, four point eight gigabytes. Checkpointing every block keeps only the twelve inputs, plus one block's internals while it is being rebuilt, one gigabyte in all, under a quarter of the original. Checkpointing every two blocks needs one point one gigabytes, and every four, one point seven five, because more blocks must be rebuilt at once. The price is that every rebuilt activation is computed twice. In total that is about one extra forward pass, and since backward costs roughly two forwards, about a third more compute per step. That is worth paying when memory, not compute, is what limits the batch size or the sequence length. One detail can break it: any dropout inside a block must draw the same mask on recomputation, and PyTorch restores the random state by default to make that so.

Before changing anything for speed, find out where the time actually goes. This is a supplied profile of one training step, ninety-two milliseconds of wall time, and it says the model is not the bottleneck. The data loader takes sixty-one milliseconds, two thirds of the step, decoding and augmenting images on the main process while the accelerator sits idle. The accelerator is busy for only thirty-four milliseconds in total, about thirty-seven percent utilisation. The call to loss dot item costs another nine milliseconds. Not because reading one number is slow, but because it forces the CPU to wait until every queued GPU operation has finished, a synchronisation point that stops the CPU from running ahead. The copy from host to device adds about four more. The fixes follow from the rows, and should go in one at a time. Four loader workers decode images in parallel with training. Pinned memory with non-blocking copies lets transfer overlap with compute. And logging the loss every fifty steps, rather than calling item every step, removes the forced wait. Then profile again, over a few warm steps rather than the first one, which includes start-up costs. Notice what would not have helped: switching to lower precision speeds up the accelerator, which here spends most of the step waiting for data.

An efficiency change is only an improvement if the model is still as good. So measure speed, memory and quality together, on the same split and the same seeds, changing one thing at a time. These are illustrative measurements at a batch of sixty-four. The fp32 baseline trains at about seven hundred images a second, peaks at three point nine gigabytes, and reaches a validation macro F one of nought point eight five one, with a spread of four thousandths over three seeds. Adding loader workers and pinned memory, the fix from the profile, raises throughput to over eighteen hundred images a second with exactly the same results. Turning on bf16 autocast raises it to nearly three thousand, cuts peak memory to two point three gigabytes, and gives nought point eight four nine, a change well inside the spread between seeds. Switching to fp16 without a gradient scaler is about as fast again, but the macro F one falls to nought point five five, with a huge spread across seeds, as small gradients underflow to zero. Two lessons follow. The biggest gain came from the input pipeline, not from precision. And the fp16 failure is invisible in the speed numbers: it shows up only in quality. Report hardware, batch, dtype, step time, peak memory and quality with seeds, every time.

Compression and parallelism go beyond a training loop on a single device, and their implementations belong to specialists and to the deployment and infrastructure teams. What this course needs is to know what each one changes, and what to check before trusting it. The fine-tuned model's weights take forty-five megabytes in fp32, twenty-two in a sixteen-bit format, and eleven in eight-bit integers. Quantisation shrinks them by changing their numerics, so the result must be re-evaluated, per class rather than by overall accuracy, because rare defect classes are often the first to suffer. Pruning and distillation change the model itself, so they need a full re-evaluation, as if it were a new model. On the parallelism side, data parallel training splits each batch across devices, which makes batch norm statistics per device unless they are synchronised, and changes the effective batch size, so the learning rate may need revisiting. Tensor and pipeline parallelism split the layers themselves across devices, and the first check is that the numbers match a single-device run. When you hand this work over, send three things with the request. The baseline: its metrics, seeds, split and exact checkpoint. The budget: the latency and memory target. And the tolerance: the largest drop in quality that would be acceptable.

A neural design is justified by the task it serves, so this last chapter starts from the task contract, not from a model. The contract for the workshop is fixed before any training. The input is one image, available at inspection time, and the output is one of three classes: ok, scratch or dent. Data is split by production batch, so no batch contributes to both training and evaluation. The metric is macro F one, with dent recall reported alongside, because dents are the costly miss. The budget is fifty milliseconds per image on the inspection station's CPU. And there is a ceiling: two inspectors agree on only ninety-two percent of images, so scores much above that mean little. Every candidate is on the list because it tests a specific assumption. Hand-made features with logistic regression, thirty-nine parameters, are the baseline that any network must clear. An MLP on raw pixels asks whether capacity alone helps. The small convolutional network from chapter six asks whether local, repeated patterns are the right bias. And a fine-tuned ResNet eighteen, from chapter ten, asks whether general visual features transfer to this camera. All four use cross-entropy, so the comparison isolates the architecture and its starting point, not the objective.

A comparison between models is only fair if every candidate gets the same split, the same seeds, the same training budget and the same search, and if all of that is declared before training starts. Otherwise the most-tuned model wins, not the best one. Here the declaration is short. Two thousand four hundred images for training and validation, and four hundred and eighty test images, with every split grouped by production batch. Three seeds, nought, one and two, with results reported as a mean and a spread. Thirty epochs with early stopping on validation macro F one, and eight trials of learning rate and weight decay for each candidate. And only label-preserving augmentation, flips and small rotations, which chapter ten showed keep a scratch visible. The splits then decide what each number may be called. Anything measured on training batches is a training observation, useful for diagnosis, never a result. Validation batches are where models are chosen, stopped and tuned. Test batches are used once, for each chosen model, at the very end, and never to make a choice. Writing the configuration into a file, with the split file beside it, means the results can be traced back to exactly what produced them, and the next comparison can reuse the same split.

The comparison covers everything the contract names, not just one quality score. Validation figures are means over three seeds, and test figures come from one final run per model. The MLP on pixels reaches only nought point six nine on validation, below the hand-feature baseline at nought point seven one, so capacity alone did not help. The small convolutional network reaches nought point eight six on validation and nought point eight five on test. The fine-tuned ResNet eighteen reaches nought point nine three on validation and nought point nine one on test. On images from station C, a station held out entirely, every model drops. The ResNet falls to nought point eight three and the small network to nought point seven one. The ResNet also recalls eighty-six percent of dents, against seventy-four for the small network, and at twenty-eight milliseconds per image on the CPU it fits inside the fifty millisecond budget. Two cautions come with the reading. The station C drop shows robustness to new stations is not solved by any candidate. And a test score of nought point nine one is already close to the ceiling set by inspector agreement. The sensor-history model answers a different question, so its evidence is reported separately. The recommendation is the fine-tuned ResNet eighteen, with station C named as a known limit.

A validation score only holds at inference if the model runs exactly as it was evaluated, and that takes more than a file of weights. The contract lists everything that must travel with it. First, the state dictionary, including the batch norm buffers, with a hash so the exact file can be verified. Second, the mode: the model must be in evaluation mode, so dropout is off and batch norm uses its stored running statistics rather than the statistics of whatever batch arrives. Third, the preprocessing: resizing to two hundred and twenty-four pixels and normalising with the mean and standard deviation stored in the checkpoint, because a different normalisation shifts every feature. Fourth, the class order. If index one means scratch in training but dent in the inspection software, every prediction is silently wrong. And fifth, the dtype, here bf16 autocast, which was validated against fp32. The same idea applies to the course's other models. A text model needs its tokeniser vocabulary file, with padding at nought and unknown at one. A sensor model needs its recurrent state reset for each machine, and the same causal and padding masks it was trained with. Enforce the contract when the model is loaded: check the hash, and read the preprocessing and the class names from the checkpoint itself.

A model recommendation is not the same as operational readiness. Offline evidence answers some questions and should name the rest, each with an owner. Five remain open here. New stations: the model scores nought point eight three on station C against nought point nine one on the test batches, so how much station data would close that gap is a question for the domain and modelling teams. Dent recall: at eighty-six percent, about one dent in seven is missed, and only the domain experts can say what a missed dent costs. The label ceiling: inspectors disagree on eight percent of images, and adjudicating those images might be worth more than any model change. Live inputs: chapter eleven showed that blank frames and lighting changes slip past reconstruction scores, so checks must run before a prediction is trusted. And drift over time: there is no evidence at all yet, because none of it can be gathered offline. The handoff package carries the checkpoint and its manifest, an evidence card with the validation, test and station C results, the split file, the budgets, and the table of known limits. The sensor model goes with its own separate evidence. Serving, monitoring and retraining are then implemented by the MLOps side, which is where the companion course picks up.

This course worked through one fictional workshop, but the habits it built carry to any problem, and the way to keep them is to practise on examples you have not seen before. Six habits matter most. Trace shapes on paper before running anything, because most bugs show up as a shape that cannot be right. Fit a baseline first, and then ask what a network actually adds over it. Split by group, whether that is production batch, machine, customer or time, so evaluation reflects what the model will face. Check visibility: what each position may see through its masks, what carried state leaks between sequences, and what preprocessing has seen the test data. Measure quality and resources together, over several seeds, changing one thing at a time. And label every number with the evidence it is: a training observation, a validation result or a final test. Several topics were deferred on purpose. The derivations behind backpropagation and optimisation belong to the maths courses. General evaluation, calibration and responsible use are covered in the Machine Learning course. Serving, monitoring and retraining belong to MLOps. And detection, segmentation, generative models, reinforcement learning and graph networks each have their own specialist courses. Take the habits with you into each one.
